name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q01 - Order of reactivity of alcohols with halogen acids

questiontext.text:
The order of reactivity of following alcohols with halogen acids is

(A) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{OH}\)

(B) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2-\underset{\substack{|\\\mathrm{CH}_3}}{\mathrm{CH}}-\mathrm{OH}\)

(C) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2-\underset{\substack{|\\\mathrm{CH}_3}}{\overset{\substack{\mathrm{CH}_3\\|}}{\mathrm{C}}}-\mathrm{OH}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The reaction of alcohols with halogen acids (\(\mathrm{HX}\)) to form alkyl halides proceeds through protonation of the hydroxyl group followed by the departure of a water molecule to generate a carbocation intermediate. The cleavage of the \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond to form the carbocation is the rate-determining step. Consequently, the reactivity of the alcohol depends on the relative stability of the intermediate carbocation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Intermediates
- The primary alcohol (\(1^\circ\)), 1-propanol (A), forms a primary carbocation, \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_2\), which has the least stabilization.
- The secondary alcohol (\(2^\circ\)), butan-2-ol (B), forms a secondary carbocation, \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{CH}_3\), stabilized by inductive donation and hyperconjugation from two alkyl groups.
- The tertiary alcohol (\(3^\circ\)), 2-methylbutan-2-ol (C), forms a tertiary carbocation, \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\mathrm{C}}(\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\), stabilized by extensive inductive donation and hyperconjugation from three alkyl groups.

Step 3: Reactivity Order
The stability of carbocations follows the sequence: tertiary (\(3^\circ\)) > secondary (\(2^\circ\)) > primary (\(1^\circ\)). Therefore, the tertiary alcohol exhibits the fastest rate, followed by the secondary alcohol, while the primary alcohol reacts most slowly.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The decreasing order of reactivity of the alcohols towards halogen acids is \((\mathrm{C}) > (\mathrm{B}) > (\mathrm{A})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q02 - Reaction of alcohols with concentrated hydrochloric acid

questiontext.text: Which of the following alcohols will yield the corresponding alkyl chloride on reaction with concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\) at room temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The conversion of an alcohol into an alkyl chloride using concentrated hydrochloric acid (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)) proceeds through an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) pathway. The rate-determining step is the loss of a water molecule from the protonated alcohol to form a carbocation intermediate.

Step 2: Comparison of Alcohol Classes
Primary and secondary alcohols produce relatively unstable carbocations; hence, their reaction with concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\) requires a catalyst such as anhydrous \(\mathrm{ZnCl}_2\) (Lucas reagent) and heating in the case of primary alcohols. Tertiary alcohols produce highly stable tertiary carbocations, allowing the substitution to occur rapidly and spontaneously with concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\) at room temperature simply upon shaking.

Step 3: Evaluation of Structures
- \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{OH}\) is a primary alcohol (\(1^\circ\)).
- \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2-\underset{\substack{|\\\mathrm{CH}_3}}{\mathrm{CH}}-\mathrm{OH}\) is a secondary alcohol (\(2^\circ\)).
- \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2-\underset{\substack{|\\\mathrm{CH}_3}}{\mathrm{CH}}-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{OH}\) is a primary alcohol (\(1^\circ\)).
- \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2-\underset{\substack{|\\\mathrm{CH}_3}}{\overset{\substack{\mathrm{CH}_3\\|}}{\mathrm{C}}}-\mathrm{OH}\) is 2-methylbutan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol (\(3^\circ\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The tertiary alcohol \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2-\underset{\substack{|\\\mathrm{CH}_3}}{\overset{\substack{\mathrm{CH}_3\\|}}{\mathrm{C}}}-\mathrm{OH}\) readily yields the corresponding tertiary alkyl chloride at room temperature upon reaction with concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q03 - Identification of product in Sandmeyer reaction

questiontext.text: Identify the compound Y in the following reaction.

Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The reaction sequence illustrates the classic Sandmeyer reaction for preparing aryl halides from primary aromatic amines.

Step 2: Diazotisation

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q04 - Reaction of toluene with halogen in presence of catalyst

questiontext.text: Toluene reacts with a halogen in the presence of iron (III) chloride giving ortho and para halo compounds. The reaction is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Halogenation of alkylarenes in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as iron (III) chloride (\(\mathrm{FeCl}_3\)) proceeds by an electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism.

Step 2: Generation of Electrophile and Directing Influence
The Lewis acid catalyst polarizes the halogen molecule, generating an electrophilic halonium species (\(\mathrm{X}^+\)):
\[ \mathrm{X}_2 + \mathrm{FeCl}_3 \longrightarrow \mathrm{X}^+ + [\mathrm{FeCl}_3\mathrm{X}]^- \]
The methyl group of toluene acts as an activating, ortho/para-directing group by inductive electron donation (+I) and hyperconjugation, directing the incoming halonium electrophile to attack the ortho and para positions of the aromatic ring.

Step 3: Mechanistic Classification
The electrophile attacks the \(\pi\)-system to form an arenium ion intermediate, followed by loss of a proton from the \(\mathrm{sp}^3\) ring carbon to restore aromaticity. Because a hydrogen atom on the ring is replaced by an electrophile, the reaction is categorized as an electrophilic substitution reaction.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The reaction is an electrophilic substitution reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q05 - Identification of halogen exchange Finkelstein reaction

questiontext.text: Which of the following is halogen exchange reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A halogen exchange reaction refers to the substitution of a halogen atom already present in a haloalkane with a different halogen atom.

Step 2: Analysis of Given Transformations
- In \(\mathrm{RX} + \mathrm{NaI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{RI} + \mathrm{NaX}\) (the Finkelstein reaction), an alkyl halide (\(\mathrm{X} = \mathrm{Cl}\) or \(\mathrm{Br}\)) reacts with sodium iodide in dry acetone to replace the halogen with iodine. This is a classic halogen exchange process.
- Addition of \(\mathrm{HX}\) to an alkene represents an electrophilic addition reaction.
- Substitution of an alcoholic hydroxyl group using \(\mathrm{HX}\) and \(\mathrm{ZnCl}_2\) represents a nucleophilic substitution of \(\mathrm{-OH}\).
- Halogenation of toluene in the presence of iron in the dark is an electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The halogen exchange reaction is \(\mathrm{RX} + \mathrm{NaI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{RI} + \mathrm{NaX}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q06 - Reagent for free radical chlorination of butane

questiontext.text:
Which reagent will you use for the following reaction?

\[ \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3 \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl} + \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CHClCH}_3 \]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The conversion of an alkane into isomeric mono-chloroalkanes is a photochemical free-radical halogenation process.

Step 2: Reaction Mechanism
Ultraviolet (\(\text{UV}\)) light provides the homolytic cleavage energy required to split chlorine molecules into highly reactive chlorine free radicals (\(\mathrm{Cl}^\bullet\)):
\[ \mathrm{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu / \text{UV}} 2\mathrm{Cl}^\bullet \]
The generated chlorine radicals abstract hydrogen atoms from butane at both the primary (\(1^\circ\)) and secondary (\(2^\circ\)) carbons, yielding 1-butyl and 2-butyl radicals, which then react with chlorine molecules to yield 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane.

Step 3: Evaluation of Alternatives
- \(\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) produces \(\mathrm{HCl}\), which is unreactive toward saturated alkanes.
- Chlorine gas in the dark lacks sufficient activation energy to dissociate into radicals at room temperature.
- Chlorine with iron in the dark is an electrophilic aromatic substitution system and does not initiate reactions with aliphatic alkanes.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The appropriate reagent and condition is \(\mathrm{Cl}_2 / \text{UV light}\).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\text{ gas in the presence of iron in dark}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q07 - Increasing order of densities of haloarenes

questiontext.text: Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their densities.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The density of aromatic compounds and haloarenes increases with an increase in molecular mass, which is directly governed by the number of halogen atoms and the atomic mass of the constituent halogen atoms.

Step 2: Comparison of the Compounds
- Compound (a) is benzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6\)), containing only carbon and hydrogen atoms, which has the lowest molecular mass and a density of approximately \(0.88\text{ g/cm}^3\).
- Compound (b) is chlorobenzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{Cl}\)), containing one chlorine atom (atomic mass \(\approx 35.5\text{ u}\)), with a density of approximately \(1.11\text{ g/cm}^3\).
- Compound (c) is 1,3-dichlorobenzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_4\mathrm{Cl}_2\)), containing two chlorine atoms, with a density of approximately \(1.29\text{ g/cm}^3\).
- Compound (d) is 1-bromo-3-chlorobenzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_4\mathrm{BrCl}\)), containing one heavy bromine atom (atomic mass \(\approx 80\text{ u}\)) and one chlorine atom, giving it the highest molecular mass and a density of approximately \(1.63\text{ g/cm}^3\).

Step 3: Density Trend
Arranging these compounds in order of increasing density gives: benzene < chlorobenzene < 1,3-dichlorobenzene < 1-bromo-3-chlorobenzene.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of densities is \((\mathrm{a}) < (\mathrm{b}) < (\mathrm{c}) < (\mathrm{d})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q08 - Increasing order of boiling points of bromobutane isomers

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their boiling points.

(a) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Br}\)

(b) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Br}\)

(c) \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{C}-\underset{\substack{|\\\mathrm{Br}}}{\overset{\substack{\mathrm{CH}_3\\|}}{\mathrm{C}}}-\mathrm{CH}_3\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For isomeric haloalkanes having the same molecular formula (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{Br}\)), boiling point depends on the magnitude of intermolecular van der Waals forces, which are directly proportional to the molecular surface area.

Step 2: Effect of Branching on Surface Area
As branching increases, the molecular shape becomes more compact and spherical. A spherical shape minimizes the surface area of contact between adjacent molecules, thereby weakening the van der Waals forces and depressing the boiling point.

Step 3: Comparison of the Isomers
- Structure (b), 1-bromobutane, is an unbranched straight-chain molecule with the maximum surface area and the strongest intermolecular attractions, resulting in the highest boiling point (\(\approx 375\text{ K}\)).
- Structure (a), 1-bromo-2-methylpropane (isobutyl bromide), possesses one methyl branch, giving an intermediate surface area and boiling point (\(\approx 364\text{ K}\)).
- Structure (c), 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide), has two methyl branches on the central carbon, adopting a compact spherical geometry with the smallest surface area and the lowest boiling point (\(\approx 346\text{ K}\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of boiling points is \((\mathrm{c}) < (\mathrm{a}) < (\mathrm{b})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q09 - Identification of asymmetric carbon in given molecules

questiontext.text:
In which of the following molecules carbon atom marked with asterisk (*) is asymmetric?

(a)

(b)

(c)

(d)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An asymmetric (or chiral) carbon atom is an \(\mathrm{sp}^3\)-hybridized carbon bonded to four entirely different atoms or groups of atoms.

Step 2: Analysis of the Four Molecules
- In molecule (a), the central carbon \(\mathrm{C}^*\) is bonded to \(\mathrm{-H}\), \(\mathrm{-Cl}\), \(\mathrm{-Br}\), and \(\mathrm{-I}\). All four attached substituents are distinct; thus, it is asymmetric.
- In molecule (b), the central carbon \(\mathrm{C}^*\) is bonded to deuterium (\(\mathrm{-D}\)), \(\mathrm{-Cl}\), \(\mathrm{-Br}\), and \(\mathrm{-I}\). All four attached substituents are distinct; thus, it is asymmetric.
- In molecule (c), the central carbon \(\mathrm{C}^*\) is bonded to \(\mathrm{-H}\), \(\mathrm{-OH}\), \(\mathrm{-CH}_3\), and \(\mathrm{-C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\). All four attached groups are distinct; thus, it is asymmetric.
- In molecule (d), the central carbon \(\mathrm{C}^*\) is bonded to two identical hydrogen atoms (\(\mathrm{-H}\)), along with \(\mathrm{-CH}_3\) and \(\mathrm{-C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\). Because two identical substituents are attached, it possesses a plane of symmetry and is not asymmetric.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The carbon atom marked with an asterisk is asymmetric in molecules (a), (b), and (c).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q10 - Enantiomeric structure of given chiral haloalkane

questiontext.text:
Which of the following structures is enantiomeric with the molecule (A) given below:

(A)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Enantiomers are stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other. In a three-dimensional representation of a chiral center, interchanging any single pair of substituents (an odd number of exchanges) inverts the stereochemical configuration, transforming a molecule into its enantiomer. Performing an even number of interchanges (or pure rotational reorientations in three-dimensional space) leaves the configuration unchanged, yielding the same molecule (homomer).

Step 2: Structural Analysis of Molecule (A)
In molecule (A), the chiral carbon is bonded to four groups: \(\mathrm{-H}\) (in plane, pointing up), \(\mathrm{-C_2H_5}\) (in plane, pointing lower-left), \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\) (dashed wedge, pointing upper-right), and \(\mathrm{-Br}\) (solid wedge, pointing lower-right).

Step 3: Evaluation of the Provided Structures
- Structure with \(\mathrm{-H}\) pointing up, \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\) in plane at the lower-left, \(\mathrm{-C_2H_5}\) on the dashed wedge at the upper-right, and \(\mathrm{-Br}\) on the solid wedge at the lower-right corresponds to exchanging the positions of the ethyl (\(\mathrm{-C_2H_5}\)) and methyl (\(\mathrm{-CH_3}\)) groups while keeping the positions of \(\mathrm{-H}\) and \(\mathrm{-Br}\) unchanged. This single interchange reverses the absolute configuration at the chiral center, producing the non-superimposable mirror image (enantiomer) of (A).
- The other structures represent identical spatial configurations (homomers) obtained by in-plane or out-of-plane rotations of molecule (A).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The structure with the single exchange of methyl and ethyl groups is enantiomeric with molecule (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q11 - Identification of vicinal dihalide among given compounds

questiontext.text: Which of the following is an example of vic-dihalide?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Vicinal dihalides (vic-dihalides) are dihalogenated organic compounds in which two halogen atoms are bonded to two adjacent (neighbouring) carbon atoms.

Step 2: Evaluation of Options
- Dichloromethane has the formula \(\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl}_2\). Both chlorine atoms are attached to the same carbon atom; hence, it is a geminal dihalide (gem-dihalide).
- 1,2-Dichloroethane has the structural formula \(\mathrm{Cl-CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{Cl}\). The two chlorine atoms are attached to adjacent carbon atoms (\(\mathrm{C}_1\) and \(\mathrm{C}_2\)); thus, it is a vicinal dihalide (vic-dihalide).
- Ethylidene chloride (1,1-dichloroethane) has the formula \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CHCl}_2\). Both chlorine atoms reside on the same carbon atom; thus, it is a geminal dihalide.
- Allyl chloride has the formula \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl}\). It contains only one halogen atom and is a monohalide.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
1,2-Dichloroethane is the example of a vic-dihalide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q12 - Classification of bromine position in unsaturated haloalkane

questiontext.text: The position of \(-\mathrm{Br}\) in the compound \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CHC}(\mathrm{Br})(\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\) can be classified as

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Halides are classified according to the nature and hybridisation of the carbon atom bearing the halogen:
- Allylic halide: The halogen atom is bonded to an \(\mathrm{sp}^3\)-hybridised carbon that is directly adjacent to a carbon-carbon double bond (\(\mathrm{C=C}\)).
- Vinylic halide: The halogen atom is bonded directly to an \(\mathrm{sp}^2\)-hybridised carbon of a carbon-carbon double bond.
- Arylic halide: The halogen atom is bonded directly to an aromatic ring.
- Secondary halide: The halogen is attached to a carbon bonded to exactly two other carbon atoms.

Step 2: Structural Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{Br})(\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\), the bromine atom is bonded to a tertiary \(\mathrm{sp}^3\)-hybridised carbon atom that is directly attached to the \(\mathrm{-CH=CH-}\) alkene group. Because the carbon bearing \(-\mathrm{Br}\) is adjacent to a \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bond, this position is allylic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The position of the bromine atom is classified as allyl.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q13 - Electrophilic species in chlorination of benzene

questiontext.text: Chlorobenzene is formed by reaction of chlorine with benzene in the presence of \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\). Which of the following species attacks the benzene ring in this reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The chlorination of benzene in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride (\(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\)) is an electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction.

Step 2: Generation of Electrophile
Aluminium chloride acts as a Lewis acid by accepting an electron pair from the chlorine molecule, thereby polarizing the \(\mathrm{Cl-Cl}\) bond and generating a chloronium electrophile (\(\mathrm{Cl}^+\)):
\[ \mathrm{Cl}_2 + \mathrm{AlCl}_3 \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cl}^+ + [\mathrm{AlCl}_4]^- \]

Step 3: Attack on the Aromatic Ring
The electron-deficient chloronium ion (\(\mathrm{Cl}^+\)) serves as the active electrophilic species that attacks the electron-dense \(\pi\)-cloud of the benzene ring to generate an arenium ion (sigma complex), followed by removal of a proton by \([\mathrm{AlCl}_4]^-\) to yield chlorobenzene and regenerate \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The species that attacks the benzene ring is the chloronium ion, \(\mathrm{Cl}^+\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q14 - Classification of ethylidene chloride as dihalide

questiontext.text: Ethylidene chloride is a/an

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dihaloalkanes are categorized based on the relative positions of the two halogen atoms:
- Geminal dihalide (gem-dihalide): Both halogen atoms are bonded to the same carbon atom. Common nomenclature names them alkylidene halides.
- Vicinal dihalide (vic-dihalide): The two halogen atoms are bonded to two adjacent carbon atoms. Common nomenclature names them alkylene dihalides.

Step 2: Identification of Ethylidene Chloride
Ethylidene chloride has the IUPAC name 1,1-dichloroethane and the condensed formula \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CHCl}_2\). Because both chlorine atoms are attached to the same carbon atom (\(\mathrm{C}_1\)), it is a geminal dihalide.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ethylidene chloride is classified as a gem-dihalide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q15 - Major product formed in electrophilic addition to allylbenzene

questiontext.text: What is ‘A’ in the following reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The addition of a hydrogen halide (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)) to an unsymmetrical alkene follows Markovnikov's rule. Electrophilic addition begins with the attack of the double bond on the proton (\(\mathrm{H}^+\)) to form the more stable carbocation intermediate.

Step 2: Protonation and Carbocation Stability
In allylbenzene, \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}_2\), protonation of the terminal carbon (\(\mathrm{CH}_2\)) produces a secondary carbocation, \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{CH}_3\), rather than an unstable primary carbocation, \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_2\).

Step 3: Nucleophilic Attack
The chloride ion (\(\mathrm{Cl}^-\)) then attacks the carbocation center at \(\mathrm{C}_2\), yielding the Markovnikov addition product, \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{Cl})-\mathrm{CH}_3\) (2-chloro-1-phenylpropane).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Product ‘A’ corresponds to \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{Cl})-\mathrm{CH}_3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q16 - Preferred nucleophilic substitution pathway for primary halides

questiontext.text: A primary alkyl halide would prefer to undergo

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleophilic substitution in alkyl halides can proceed via a bimolecular (\(\mathrm{S_N2}\)) or a unimolecular (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\)) pathway.

Step 2: Analysis of Primary Alkyl Halides
- Steric Factor: In primary alkyl halides (\(\mathrm{R-CH}_2\mathrm{-X}\)), the carbon bonded to the halogen is attached to only one alkyl group and two hydrogen atoms. Steric hindrance is minimal, allowing an incoming nucleophile to easily perform a backside attack on the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) \(\sigma^*\) orbital.
- Electronic Factor: The ionization of a primary alkyl halide requires very high activation energy because primary carbocations are highly unstable and lack sufficient hyperconjugative stabilization. Hence, the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism is disfavored.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Due to low steric crowding and the instability of primary carbocations, a primary alkyl halide preferentially undergoes an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q17 - Alkyl halide undergoing unimolecular substitution most readily

questiontext.text: Which of the following alkyl halides will undergo \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction most readily?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The unimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\)) mechanism involves the heterolytic cleavage of the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond as the slow, rate-determining step to generate a carbocation intermediate. When the alkyl group is identical (here, the tertiary butyl group, \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{C}-\)), the reaction rate is governed by the bond dissociation enthalpy of the carbon-halogen bond and the leaving group ability of the halide ion.

Step 2: Comparison of Leaving Groups and Bond Enthalpies
As we descend Group 17 from fluorine to iodine, the size of the halogen atom increases, leading to longer and weaker \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bonds:
- Bond dissociation enthalpy follows the order: \(\mathrm{C-F} > \mathrm{C-Cl} > \mathrm{C-Br} > \mathrm{C-I}\).
- Leaving group ability follows the reverse order: \(\mathrm{I}^- > \mathrm{Br}^- > \mathrm{Cl}^- > \mathrm{F}^-\), because iodide is a very weak base with high polarizability, stabilizing the negative charge effectively.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond is the weakest and iodide is the best leaving group, \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{I}\) undergoes the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction most readily.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q18 - Correct IUPAC nomenclature for branched alkyl bromide

questiontext.text: Which is the correct IUPAC name for \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\underset{\substack{|\\\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5}}{\mathrm{CH}}-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{Br}\) ?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Longest Carbon Chain Selection
Expanding the ethyl group (\(\mathrm{-C_2H_5} = \mathrm{-CH_2-CH_3}\)) gives the structure: \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{Br}\). The longest continuous carbon chain containing the carbon bonded to the principal functional substituent (\(-\mathrm{Br}\)) has 4 carbon atoms, making the parent alkane butane.

Step 2: Numbering the Parent Chain
Number the carbon chain from the end closer to the substituent with the lowest locant:
- \(\mathrm{C}_1\): \(\mathrm{-CH}_2\mathrm{Br}\)
- \(\mathrm{C}_2\): \(\mathrm{-CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)-\)
- \(\mathrm{C}_3\): \(\mathrm{-CH}_2-\)
- \(\mathrm{C}_4\): \(\mathrm{-CH}_3\)
This numbering gives locant 1 to the bromo substituent and locant 2 to the methyl substituent.

Step 3: Alphabetical Prefixes and Full Name
Listing the prefixes in alphabetical order: "1-bromo" precedes "2-methyl". Combining with the parent name butane gives 1-bromo-2-methylbutane.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct IUPAC name is 1-bromo-2-methylbutane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q19 - Correct IUPAC nomenclature for diethylbromomethane

questiontext.text: What should be the correct IUPAC name for diethylbromomethane?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural Representation
The common name diethylbromomethane indicates a methane carbon atom bonded to two ethyl groups, one bromine atom, and one hydrogen atom: \(\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5)_2\mathrm{Br}\). Expanding the ethyl groups gives the structural formula: \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{Br})-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_3\).

Step 2: Parent Chain and Numbering
The longest continuous carbon chain consists of 5 carbon atoms, so the parent hydrocarbon is pentane. Numbering from either end gives the central carbon bearing the bromine atom the locant 3.

Step 3: Full IUPAC Name
With the bromo substituent at position 3 of a pentane chain, the correct systematic IUPAC name is 3-bromopentane.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct IUPAC name is 3-bromopentane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q20 - Reaction of toluene with chlorine in dark with iron

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q21 - Reaction of chloromethane with excess ammonia

In Hofmann's ammonolysis of alkyl halides, ammonia acts as a nucleophile to displace the halide ion, initially generating a primary amine. The primary amine itself possesses a lone pair of electrons and can act as a nucleophile to react with remaining alkyl halide, leading successively to secondary and tertiary amines, and eventually quaternary ammonium salts.

Step 2: Effect of Reagent Proportions
When ammonia is present in large excess relative to chloromethane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{Cl}\)), the probability of a chloromethane molecule colliding with an ammonia molecule is overwhelmingly higher than colliding with an already formed primary amine molecule. Consequently, further alkylation is suppressed.

Step 3: Final Conclusion

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q22 - Identification of chiral haloalkane molecule

A molecule is chiral if it lacks an alternating axis of symmetry (most commonly planes or centres of symmetry) and possesses a non-superimposable mirror image. In organic chemistry, a tetrahedral carbon atom bonded to four entirely different atoms or groups is an asymmetric (chiral) centre, conferring chirality to simple mono-haloalkanes.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q23 - Mechanism of hydrolysis of benzyl bromide

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q26 - Rate of nucleophilic aromatic substitution with nitro group

Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleophilic aromatic substitution in haloarenes occurs via an addition-elimination mechanism involving a negatively charged Meisenheimer complex intermediate. Electron-withdrawing groups such as \(\mathrm{-NO}_2\) at ortho and para positions strongly stabilize the carbanion intermediate by resonance (-R) and inductive (-I) effects, dramatically increasing the reaction rate relative to unsubstituted chlorobenzene.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q27 - Influence of electron-releasing methyl group on nucleophilic substitution

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution proceeds via a carbanionic Meisenheimer intermediate. Electron-donating groups like methyl (\(\mathrm{-CH}_3\)) donate electron density via inductive (+I) and hyperconjugative effects, which destabilizes the negatively charged intermediate and decreases the rate of nucleophilic substitution. In addition, ortho substituents exert steric hindrance to incoming nucleophiles.

- In 3-chlorotoluene (c), the methyl group is meta to chlorine. Electron donation by hyperconjugation does not deliver electron density directly to the ipso carbon, but its +I effect still destabilizes the intermediate relative to unsubstituted chlorobenzene, making it intermediate in rate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The rate of nucleophilic substitution increases in the order: \((\mathrm{b}) < (\mathrm{c}) < (\mathrm{a})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q29 - Retarding effect of multiple methyl groups on nucleophilic substitution

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q30 - Increasing order of boiling points for butane and butyl halides

questiontext.text:
Which is the correct increasing order of boiling points of the following compounds?

1-Iodobutane, 1-Bromobutane, 1-Chlorobutane, Butane

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Boiling points of organic compounds depend on the strength of intermolecular attractive forces. For haloalkanes of the same alkyl group, intermolecular dipole-dipole interactions and London dispersion forces increase systematically with an increase in the size and polarizability of the halogen atom and the overall molecular mass.

Step 2: Comparison of the Compounds
- Unsubstituted butane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_{10}\)) is non-polar and exhibits only weak dispersion forces with a low molecular mass (\(58\text{ g/mol}\)), giving it the lowest boiling point.
- For the 1-halobutanes, halogen size, polarizability, and molecular weight increase in the sequence \(\mathrm{Cl} < \mathrm{Br} < \mathrm{I}\). As a result, dispersion forces strengthen in the order: 1-chlorobutane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{Cl}\)) < 1-bromobutane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{Br}\)) < 1-iodobutane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{I}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of boiling points is: Butane < 1-Chlorobutane < 1-Bromobutane < 1-Iodobutane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q31 - Increasing order of boiling points of bromo derivatives

The boiling point of homologous halogenated compounds increases with increasing chain length and molecular mass because London dispersion forces scale directly with molecular surface area and the total number of polarizable electrons. In addition, aromatic haloarenes possess a large planar \(\pi\)-electron cloud with high polarizability, leading to particularly strong intermolecular dispersion forces.

Step 2: Comparison of the Compounds
- For the aliphatic bromoalkanes, the chain length increases from ethyl to propyl to butyl. Consequently, boiling point increases in the order: 1-bromoethane (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{Br}\), molar mass \(109\text{ g/mol}\)) < 1-bromopropane (\(\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{H}_7\mathrm{Br}\), molar mass \(123\text{ g/mol}\)) < 1-bromobutane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{Br}\), molar mass \(137\text{ g/mol}\)).
- Bromobenzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{Br}\), molar mass \(157\text{ g/mol}\)) has the highest molecular mass and a large planar delocalized aromatic ring, imparting the strongest dispersion interactions and the highest boiling point.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of boiling points is: 1-Bromoethane < 1-Bromopropane < 1-Bromobutane < Bromobenzene.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q37 - Identification of haloalkanes with sp3 hybridized carbon

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q38 - Properties and reactions of ethylene and ethylidene chloride isomers

questiontext.text: Ethylene chloride and ethylidene chloride are isomers. Identify the correct statements.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ethylene chloride (1,2-dichloroethane, \(\mathrm{ClCH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl}\)) is a vicinal dihalide, whereas ethylidene chloride (1,1-dichloroethane, \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHCl}_2\)) is a geminal dihalide. Because their chlorine atoms are positioned differently on the carbon chain, they are positional isomers, not chain isomers.

Step 2: Analysis of the Chemical Reactions
- Dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\): Both undergo two successive \(\beta\)-elimination reactions of \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to yield the same alkyne, ethyne (\(\mathrm{CH}\equiv\mathrm{CH}\)):
\[ \mathrm{ClCH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl} + 2\,\text{alc. }\mathrm{KOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HC}\equiv\mathrm{CH} + 2\,\mathrm{KCl} + 2\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \]
\[ \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHCl}_2 + 2\,\text{alc. }\mathrm{KOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HC}\equiv\mathrm{CH} + 2\,\mathrm{KCl} + 2\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \]
Thus, both form ethyne with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\).
- Reduction: Complete reduction with zinc and hydrochloric acid or \(\mathrm{H}_2/\mathrm{Ni}\) removes both chlorine atoms, yielding the parent alkane, ethane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_3\)), from both isomers.
- Hydrolysis with aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\): Ethylene chloride gives ethane-1,2-diol (glycol), whereas ethylidene chloride gives ethanal (acetaldehyde), producing different products upon hydrolysis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that both compounds form ethyne on treatment with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\), and both form ethane on reduction.

Standard metallic fluorides utilized for the Swarts reaction include silver fluoride (\(\mathrm{AgF}\)), mercurous fluoride (\(\mathrm{Hg}_2\mathrm{F}_2\)), cobalt(II) fluoride (\(\mathrm{CoF}_2\)), and antimony trifluoride (\(\mathrm{SbF}_3\)).
In contrast, ionic alkali/alkaline-earth fluorides such as \(\mathrm{NaF}\) and \(\mathrm{CaF}_2\) are not suitable for this transformation due to high lattice enthalpy and unfavourable solubility.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The appropriate metallic fluorides among the choices are \(\mathrm{CoF}_2\) and \(\mathrm{Hg}_2\mathrm{F}_2\).
